title: فعل الكينونة (ser/estar) وأشكاله / Verb to be (ser/estar) and its forms
bridge: In Spanish, the verbs 'ser' or 'estar' are essential and always appear in a sentence. In Arabic, however, the verb 'to be' is not expressed in the present tense: it is omitted, and the sentence is formed simply with a subject and a predicate. For example, 'Ahmad is a student' is said as 'أحمد طالب' (literally 'Ahmad student'). This absence can be surprising at first, but it is a simple and very useful rule. Remember that in the past tense, the verb 'كان' (to be) is used, marking a key difference with Spanish.
rule: In Arabic, the verb 'to be' in the present tense is neither written nor pronounced. The nominal sentence (جملة اسمية) consists of a subject (مبتدأ) and a predicate (خبر), both in the nominative case. To express 'to be' in the present tense, simply juxtapose the subject and the predicate. Examples: 'أنا طالب' (I am a student), 'هي طبيبة' (She is a doctor). To negate the present tense, 'ليس' (for third-person masculine) or 'ليست' (feminine) is used before the predicate. Example: 'أنا لست طالباً' (I am not a student). In the past tense, 'كان' (was) and its variants are used: 'كانت' (she was), 'كنت' (I was). In the future tense, 'سيكون' (will be) is used. At the A1 level, it is essential to master the present tense form without a verb and recognize the basic past forms of 'كان'.

common_error.wrong: أنا أكون طالب (Trying to translate 'I am a student' using an explicit verb)
common_error.correct_alt: أكون طالباً (in specific contexts, but not in simple present)
common_error.explanation: The most common mistake is adding an explicit 'to be' verb in the present tense (such as 'أكون', which is a form of the verb 'كان') because Spanish speakers are used to the presence of the verb. In Arabic, the nominal sentence does not include a copular verb in the present tense. To avoid this, remember that in the present tense, if you want to say 'X is Y', simply say X Y. Practice with simple phrases like 'أنا مهندس' (I am an engineer) and 'هي جميلة' (she is beautiful).

title: الضمائر الشخصية / Personal pronouns
bridge: In Spanish, personal pronouns are essential, but in Arabic they are often omitted because the verb already indicates the person. However, when used, they have specific forms for gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/dual/plural). Unlike Spanish, Arabic has a dual pronoun (we two/you two) that does not exist in Spanish. Additionally, the pronoun 'she' (هي) is also used for inanimate feminine objects, similar to Spanish 'ella' but more broadly.
rule: The personal pronouns in Modern Standard Arabic are: أنا (ana) = I, أنتَ (anta) = you (masculine), أنتِ (anti) = you (feminine), هو (huwa) = he, هي (hiya) = she, نحن (naḥnu) = we, أنتم (antum) = you (masculine or mixed), أنتن (antunna) = you (feminine), هم (hum) = they (masculine), هن (hunna) = they (feminine). There is no equivalent to the neutral 'it' in Arabic; objects and concepts are treated as masculine or feminine. At the A1 level, we focus on singular and plural, leaving the dual for later levels. In formal contexts, 'أنتم' is used for 'you' (plural), and 'أنتما' for 'you two' (dual), but this is not essential at A1.

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, we sometimes say 'yo soy estudiante' and might think we need the pronoun 'él' for 'ser', but in Arabic the verb 'to be' is implied in nominal sentences. Adding 'هو' (he) after 'أنا' is a common mistake because we translate literally from Spanish. Arabic nominal sentences simply connect subject and predicate without needing a verb. Avoid adding extra pronouns.

title: أل التعريف (Al- at-ta'rif) / The definite article
bridge: In Spanish, we use 'el/la/los/las' for definite articles and 'un/una/unos/unas' for indefinite ones. In Arabic, only the definite article 'al-' (ال) exists, which is prefixed to the word, and there is no indefinite article: indefiniteness is marked with the '-n' ending (tanwin) on nouns and adjectives. Additionally, 'al-' assimilates with certain solar consonants (like t, d, r, s), changing its pronunciation, which has no parallel in Spanish.
rule: The definite article in Arabic is the prefix 'al-' (ال) added to the beginning of a noun or adjective. For example, 'kitāb' (book) becomes 'al-kitāb' (the book). When the word begins with a solar consonant (ت، ث، د، ذ، ر، ز، س، ش، ص، ض، ط، ظ، ل، ن), the 'l' in 'al-' assimilates and the initial consonant is doubled, pronounced as, for example, 'ash-shams' (the sun) instead of 'al-shams'. Indefiniteness is expressed through the '-n' ending (tanwin) on nouns and adjectives, which is written (though not always in fully vocalized texts) and pronounced. For example, 'kitābun' (a book). In nominal sentences, the adjective agrees with the noun in definiteness: if the noun has 'al-', the adjective does too; if it is indefinite, both take tanwin. Unlike Spanish, there are no special plural forms for the article; 'al-' is used the same way with singulars, plurals, and feminine nouns.

title: الجنس والعدد في الأسماء / Gender and number of nouns
bridge: In Spanish, nouns have gender (masculine/feminine) and number (singular/plural). In Arabic, the system is similar but with key differences: feminine is almost always marked by the ending ة (ta marbuta), and plural has two types: regular plural and broken plural (internal change), which alters the word internally. Additionally, in Arabic, adjectives must agree in gender and number, and the dual (for two things) is a mandatory category that does not exist in Spanish.
rule: In Arabic, nouns have gender (مذكر/مؤنث) and number (مفرد/مثنى/جمع). The feminine gender is generally formed by adding ة (ta marbuta) to the masculine (e.g. معلم -> معلمة). Some nouns are feminine without ة (e.g. أم, شمس), and some are masculine but refer to feminine beings (e.g. امرأة). The dual number is used for exactly two items, formed by adding انِ (masculine) or تانِ (feminine) to the singular. The regular masculine plural adds ونَ (nominative) or ينَ (accusative/genitive); the feminine regular plural adds ات. The broken plural (جمع تكسير) changes the internal structure of the word (e.g. كتاب -> كتب). In A1, we focus on singular and basic plural (regular and some common broken plurals). Adjectives agree with nouns in gender, number, and case, but for A1 we cover singular and plural without cases.

common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers tend to use 'هذا' (this) for everything, but in Arabic, a distinction must be made between 'هذا' (masculine) and 'هذه' (feminine). 'مدرسة' is feminine, so it requires 'هذه'. It is important to pay attention to the noun's gender when choosing the correct demonstrative.

title: الفِعْل المُضارِع المرفوع / Present indicative
bridge: In Arabic, present verbs are conjugated using prefixes and suffixes that indicate person, number, and gender, unlike Spanish where we only use endings. Additionally, Arabic distinguishes between masculine and feminine in the second and third person singular and plural, which does not occur in Spanish. At first, it can be confusing that ‘you’ masculine and ‘you’ feminine are conjugated differently, but it is essential for speaking correctly.
rule: The regular present in Arabic is formed with the verb root (three consonants) and adding a prefix and suffix according to the person. Let's take the verb كَتَبَ (kataba - to write) as an example. Its present form is يَكْتُبُ (yaktubu) with the following forms: أَكْتُبُ (aktubu) - I write; تَكْتُبُ (taktubu) - you (masc.) / you (formal) write; تَكْتُبِينَ (taktubīna) - you (fem.) / you (formal) write; يَكْتُبُ (yaktubu) - he / you (formal) write; تَكْتُبُ (taktubu) - she / you (formal) write; نَكْتُبُ (naktubu) - we write; تَكْتُبُونَ (taktubūna) - you (masc. pl.) / you (formal pl.) write; تَكْتُبْنَ (taktubna) - you (fem. pl.) / you (formal pl.) write; يَكْتُبُونَ (yaktubūna) - they (masc.) / you (formal pl.) write; يَكْتُبْنَ (yaktubna) - they (fem.) / you (formal pl.) write. Note that at the end of the verb in the present, there is usually a vowel (u) or a suffix like -na. There is no specific form for ‘you all’ in Modern Standard Arabic; the same conjugation is used as for ‘you’ (formal). Verbs ending in a vowel (like نَسِيَ, nasiya - to forget) or those with weak consonants follow other patterns, but for A1 we focus on regular verbs.

common_error.explanation: Many Spanish speakers tend to use the third person singular (يَكْتُبُ) for all persons at the beginning because in Spanish the first person singular is easily distinguished. In Arabic, the first person singular takes the prefix أَ (a-) and the third person takes يَ (ya-). It is important to memorize the prefixes for each person to avoid confusion.

title: النفي الأساسي / Basic negation
bridge: In Spanish, we use 'no' before the verb to negate ('no soy', 'no tengo'). In Arabic, negation varies depending on the verb tense and sentence type: we use 'لا' for present, 'ما' for past, and 'لَيْسَ' for nominal sentences (without a verb). This may seem strange at first, but it's one of the first important differences you need to master. A common mistake is using 'لا' in all cases when you actually need specific forms.
rule:
In Arabic, negation depends on the temporal context and whether the sentence is verbal or nominal.

1. **Negating the present (indicative):** Use the particle **لا** (lā) before the present tense verb. Example: لا أَذْهَبُ (lā ʾaḏhabu) = 'I do not go'.

2. **Negating the past:** Use the particle **ما** (mā) before the past tense verb. Example: ما ذَهَبْتُ (mā ḏahabtu) = 'I did not go'. You can also use **لَمْ** (lam) with the verb in the apocopated form (present without final vowel), but for A1 we focus on **ما**.

3. **Negating nominal sentences (without a verb):** Use the verb **لَيْسَ** (laysa), which agrees with the subject (like a verb 'to be'). Example: لَسْتُ طَالِبًا (lastu ṭāliban) = 'I am not a student'.

**Forms of ليس:**
- أنا: لَسْتُ (lastu)
- أنتَ (m): لَسْتَ (lasta)
- أنتِ (f): لَسْتِ (lasti)
- هو: لَيْسَ (laysa)
- هي: لَيْسَتْ (laysat)
- نحن: لَسْنَا (lasnā)

**Typical use:** To negate adjectives, professions, belongings, and states, we use 'ليس'. To negate present actions, 'لا'. To negate past actions, 'ما'.

**Note:** In spoken Arabic, negation may differ, but for Modern Standard Arabic this rule is fundamental.

concept_examples.translation: I do not write the lesson.
I did not go to school.

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'no soy estudiante' is formed with 'no' + verb. When translating literally, many students say 'أنا لا طالب' (ana lā ṭālib), which is incorrect because 'لا' is not used to negate nominal sentences without a verb. The correct form is to use the verb 'ليس' (agreeing with the subject) and change the predicate word to accusative case (ending -an for indefinite). Remember that in Arabic, negation of a nominal sentence is done with the verb 'ليس', not with the particle 'لا'.

title: الأسئلة الأساسية / Basic Questions
bridge: In Arabic, yes/no questions are formed by adding the particle هَل (hal) or أ (a) at the beginning of the affirmative sentence, without changing the word order. Unlike Spanish, rising intonation alone is not the only marker, though it can help. Wh-questions (who, what, where, when, why, how) are formed using specific interrogative words (مَن، ماذا، أين، متى، لماذا، كيف) that are generally placed at the beginning of the sentence, similar to Spanish. Be careful: in colloquial Arabic, these particles are often omitted, but in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), they are essential.
rule: For yes/no questions in Modern Standard Arabic, use 'هل' (hal) or 'أ' (a) at the beginning of the sentence. 'هل' is more common and can be used with any verb or nominal phrase. The structure is: 'هل + affirmative sentence' (e.g., هل أنت طالب؟ - Are you a student?). For information questions, use the following interrogative words: 'مَن' (man) = who, 'ماذا' (maadha) = what, 'أين' (ayna) = where, 'متى' (mataa) = when, 'لماذا' (limaadha) = why, 'كيف' (kayfa) = how. These words are placed at the beginning of the sentence, followed by the verb or subject (depending on context). In Arabic, the word order in questions can be Verb-Subject-Object (VSO) instead of the SVO common in Spanish. For 'what' questions, sometimes 'ما' (maa) is used instead of 'ماذا', especially in nominal constructions. At the A1 level, focus on the most basic forms: 'ما هذا؟' (What is this?), 'من أنت؟' (Who are you?), 'أين أنت؟' (Where are you?). Remember that the verb 'to be' is not explicitly expressed in the present tense in Arabic; it is implied.

common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers tend to omit the interrogative particle because in Spanish, rising intonation alone marks the question in these cases. In Modern Standard Arabic, it is necessary to use 'هل' or 'أ' at the beginning of the sentence to indicate that it is a yes/no question. Omitting it can confuse the listener, as the phrase could be interpreted as a statement. Always remember to include the particle in written and formal spoken Arabic.

title: الأرقام من ١ إلى ١٠٠ / Numbers from 1 to 100
bridge: In Spanish, numbers from 1 to 100 follow a fairly regular pattern, but in Arabic, you need to consider that the system is decimal and written from right to left. Additionally, numbers from 1 to 10 agree in gender with the noun they accompany, which is a new concept for Spanish speakers. Another key difference is that in Arabic, a period (٫) is used to separate decimals and a comma (٬) for thousands, the opposite of Spanish. Pay attention also to the pronunciation of compound numbers, as they are formed differently.
rule: Numbers from 1 to 10 in Arabic have masculine and feminine forms. The masculine form is used with feminine nouns and vice versa (inverted gender agreement). For example, to say 'three books', you use 'ثلاثة كتب' (thalatha kutub) because 'book' (كتاب) is masculine, but you use 'ثلاث' (thalath) for feminine nouns like 'three chairs' (ثلاث كراسي). From 11 to 19, they are formed with the unit followed by 'عشر' (ashar) or 'عشرة' (ashara) depending on gender, and the noun is in singular accusative (though simplified at A1 level). From 20 to 99, the tens are invariable (do not change gender): عشرون (ishrun) for 20, ثلاثون (thalathun) for 30, etc. Compound numbers (e.g., 21) are formed with the ten and unit coordinated with 'wa' (and), and the noun is in singular accusative. The number 100 is مئة (mi'a) or مائة (mi'a) and is also invariable.

Since 'طاولة' (table) is feminine, the number must be in the feminine form, which is 'ثلاث' (thalāth). The form 'ثلاثة' is masculine and is used with masculine nouns. Remember that the rule is the opposite of what you might expect: if the noun is feminine, you use the 'masculine' form of the number, and vice versa. A tip: 'ثلاث' is used with feminine nouns and 'ثلاثة' with masculine ones.

title: الأساسية والموافقة / Basic Adjectives and Agreement
bridge: In Spanish, adjectives agree with nouns in gender and number (e.g., 'casa grande', 'casas grandes'). In Arabic, adjectives also agree in gender and number, but there are key differences: the adjective comes after the noun (not before), and gender is marked in the word itself with the ending '-a' for feminine (e.g., 'kabīr' vs. 'kabīra'). Additionally, Arabic has two grammatical numbers (singular and plural), but the plural of adjectives follows special rules, especially for non-human things. Note that adjectives in Arabic change according to the gender and number of the noun, but they do not have a neuter form as in Spanish.
rule: In Arabic, the qualifying adjective (النعت) follows the noun it modifies and agrees with it in gender (masculine/feminine), number (singular/plural), and case (though at A1 level we focus on nominative/indefinite). For masculine singular, the base form is the dictionary form (e.g. كبير - kabīr, 'big'). For feminine singular, the masculine form is extended with the ending -a (ة) (e.g. كبيرة - kabīra, 'big' fem.). For plural: if the noun is human, the adjective can be plural (masculine with -ūn, feminine with -āt). If the noun is non-human (thing or animal), the adjective is put in feminine singular (e.g. بيوت كبيرة - buyūt kabīra, 'big houses' – literally 'a big house' agreeing). This is a common error for Spanish speakers. Key examples: masculine singular (كتاب كبير - kitāb kabīr, 'big book'), feminine singular (سيارة كبيرة - sayyāra kabīra, 'big car'), non-human plural (كتب كبيرة - kutub kabīra, 'big books' – the adjective in feminine singular).

common_error.explanation: The typical error is using the feminine form of the adjective with a masculine noun. In Spanish, 'grande' does not change with gender, but in Arabic it does. To avoid this, identify the gender of the noun: if it is masculine (كِتَاب - kitāb, 'book'), the adjective must be masculine (كَبِير - kabīr). A strategy: memorize the adjective with its feminine form, and whenever you see a noun, ask yourself whether it is masculine or feminine.

title: الملكية / Possessives
bridge: In Spanish, possessives (mi, tu, su...) agree with the possessed object (mi casa, mis casas) and sometimes with the possessor (nuestro, nuestra). In Arabic, possessives are expressed as suffixes added to the end of the noun, and these suffixes indicate the possessor (my, your, his...). There is no gender distinction in the plural (nuestro/nuestra is the same), and the noun always carries the definite article (ال) when used with a possessive, which does not happen in Spanish.
rule: In Arabic, possession is indicated by adding a pronominal suffix to the noun. The noun must carry the definite article (ال). The suffixes for each person are: -ِي (my), -كَ (your, masc.), -كِ (your, fem.), -هُ (his), -هَا (her), -نَا (our), -كُمْ (your, masc. plural), -كُنَّ (your, fem. plural), -هُمْ (their, masc.), -هُنَّ (their, fem.). In A1, we focus on the most common ones: -ِي, -كَ, -كِ, -هُ, -هَا, -نَا. Example: بَيْت (house) → بَيْتِي (my house), بَيْتُكَ (your house), بَيْتُهُ (his house). The suffix does not change form based on the noun's gender, only according to the possessor. In the plural, the form is the same for both genders (except in forms for 'you all'/'they'). The possessive is not used with particles like 'de' (as in Spanish 'la casa de Juan'), but rather the 'idafa' construction is used (not covered in A1), though the suffixes are the most direct form.

common_error.wrong: بَيْت مِي (bait mi) - using 'mi' as a separate word
common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers tend to use a separate possessive word (like 'mi' in Spanish) before the noun. In Arabic, the possessive is a suffix directly attached to the noun. Additionally, the noun must carry the definite article, but when adding the suffix, the article is not written, though it is implied. Practice attaching the suffix directly to the end of the word.
